summary:
Mission Design Lab is a browser game we built for the NASA Space Apps Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players plan their own space mission, then run it. They pick one of five destinations (Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars, asteroid Bennu or Jupiter’s moon Europa), build a spacecraft from about 30 parts within a budget and a launch-mass limit, survive random events like solar storms and power loss, and finally fly the arrival in real-time 3D.

It meets the challenge by making mission design the gameplay. Distances and sunlight levels come from NASA fact sheets, and the rocket equation and inverse-square law decide whether a design works. Players quickly learn why Mars is far, why Europa is dark, and why every kilogram counts. When a mission fails, the game explains why.

This matters because real missions are won through trade-offs in mass, power, fuel and budget, a side of exploration most people never see. Our game makes that thinking free, instant and playable in any browser, helping inspire the next generation of engineers and scientists.
details:
🚀 Mission Design Lab

Can you design a space mission that actually works?

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

🎯 The Idea in One Line

Most space games ask, "Can you shoot fast?" We asked, "Can you plan smart?"

In Mission Design Lab you build the spacecraft first, launch it, and then fly the final approach yourself. Whatever you chose on the build screen decides whether you survive.

🛠️ What It Does and How It Works

Four steps, from idea to landing.

Step

What the player does

What's happening underneath

1. Pick a mission

Choose from 5 destinations: Earth orbit, Moon, Mars, asteroid Bennu, or Jupiter's moon Europa

Each card shows real NASA numbers: sunlight, distance, signal delay

2. Build the spacecraft

Choose from about 30 parts (cameras, radar, solar panels, RTGs, engines, fuel tanks, shields) within a budget and a weight limit

Every part costs mass, power and money. You can't take everything

3. Survive the mission

Watch it run through 8 phases, from launch to completion. Solar storms, power drops and broken antennas strike at random

The game checks whether your design can handle them

4. Fly the approach

Steer a real-time 3D flight through gates and obstacles, or use autopilot at a cost to accuracy

The final score depends on science, efficiency, safety and budget

Two real physics rules run the whole game:

  • 🔥 The rocket equation: extra fuel adds weight, and weight needs more fuel. Each kilogram buys you less.
  • ☀️ The inverse-square law: the farther you are from the Sun, the weaker your solar panels and your signal. Europa gets about 1/27th of Earth's sunlight.

If a mission fails, the game tells you why, for example "Your Δv is too low, add more fuel." So players learn engineering from their failures.

🧠 What Factors Did We Consider?

We're students, so we kept asking ourselves, "Would this actually work, and would someone enjoy it?"

  • Scientific accuracy: We used real NASA fact sheets for distances and sunlight, and real physics formulas. We simplified costs and part stats on purpose so the game stays playable, and we say so openly.
  • Learning through play: Every trade-off teaches something. No lectures, just consequences.
  • Difficulty curve: Earth is the forgiving tutorial. Europa is brutal. The difficulty rises with real-world mission difficulty.
  • Making each mission different: Mars is about distance, Bennu is about precision, and Europa is about radiation and darkness. No two missions play the same.
  • Fairness: Failures always have a reason the player can understand and fix.
  • Accessibility: It works on desktop and touch screens, supports reduced-motion settings, and uses screen-reader labels.
  • Zero friction: Players don't need to install anything or create an account. They just open the website link in their browser and play.
  • Trustworthy data: We cite every NASA source and clearly separate real facts from gameplay simplifications.

🎯 Intended Impact

  • 🎓 Show how real missions are planned. Missions are won or lost on trade-offs among mass, power, fuel and budget, long before launch.
  • 🌍 Make NASA's challenges feel real. Players feel why Mars is far and why Europa is dark and dangerous.
  • 🙌 Open space engineering to everyone. It's free, instant, and needs no background knowledge.
  • 💡 Spark STEM curiosity. It connects classroom physics to real missions like OSIRIS-REx, Europa Clipper and the Mars rovers.

💻 What We Used

Category

Tools

Languages

HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript (no frameworks or libraries)

Graphics

HTML5 Canvas, a custom 3D engine we wrote for the flight section, SVG for spacecraft art

Sound

Web Audio API: every sound effect is generated by code, with no audio files

Browser features

localStorage (saves best scores), vibration on touch devices, reduced-motion support

Fonts

Google Fonts: B612 (designed for aircraft cockpits), B612 Mono, Chakra Petch

Hosting

Deployed as a static website, so it runs on any device with a modern browser

AI partner

Claude (Anthropic): we used it to design, build and refine the game

Data

NASA fact sheets, mission pages, JPL Small-Body Database (full source list included)

Hardware

Any laptop, desktop, tablet or phone with a modern browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari) and a stable internet connection. Recommended: a laptop or desktop with 4 GB RAM or more, a screen of 1280×720 or larger, and a keyboard and mouse for the 3D flight section. Touch screens are supported too.

The game is a lightweight website: nothing to download, no setup, no account. Just open the link and play.

✨ What Makes It Creative?

  1. Engineering is the game. The "boss fight" is a power budget.
  2. Your build screen decides your flight. Fuel, shielding and navigation parts you picked earlier directly change how the approach goes.
  3. Everything is made by code. Planets, nebulae, spacecraft art and sound are generated rather than imported, which keeps it small, fast and fully ours.
  4. Mission-control atmosphere. Codenames (TERRA-01, SELENE-02, ARES-03, OSIRIS-04, EUROPA-05), live telemetry and a Deep Space Network ticker make players feel like part of the team.
  5. Failure teaches. Instead of "Game Over," you get a debrief on what went wrong and how to fix it.

📌 Final Note

Our costs and part stats are simplified for gameplay, but the physics and destination data are real. We built Mission Design Lab to show that space exploration isn't just about rockets, it's about making smart decisions.
